beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe by looking at its output.
beats.got: Output looks fine whether or not the agent is safe, so you need a separate check.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Apply a mitigation (scope, split, filter, gate, review) on top of normal company controls and see how residual risk shifts
beats.got: There is a list of verbs and five mitigations. No cost or payback is mentioned anywhere.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I should be asking what could go wrong before I let this near a real stakeholder. That is a fair question.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The model writes text, and the runtime turns it into an action. Fine, but it is a mechanism lesson I did not ask for.

beats.trigger: that specific, uncomfortable, *I'd like to know and I don't* feeling, is the most plain thing in the room today.
beats.got: The module is built around a feeling. I do not do feelings, I do numbers.

beats.trigger: The story works because classical software is deterministic (same input, same output).
beats.got: Ordinary software gives the same result every time, so you can prove a fix. Agents do not.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: A document the agent reads can talk it into doing harm with access it already has. That is a real risk for finance data.

beats.trigger: Neither lens makes you an expert. The reusable check is the expert.
beats.got: The loop is assess, mitigate, reassess. It reads like a standard risk register with new names.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door. Those are the two options.
beats.got: There are two honest outcomes. You accept the risk in writing or you stop. I can take that to the board.

beats.trigger: Nobody hands you the number. You pick it, you write down what is left, and you sign for it.
beats.got: Less access means less usefulness, and a person has to sign for the trade-off. Fair, though there is still no number.

beats.trigger: It costs whoever sells you agents too, this training included: an agent that reaches less is a smaller thing to sell, and it is still the right call.
beats.got: The trainer says the cheapest mitigation is to not connect the thing, even though that hurts their own sales. That makes me trust them more.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Time:** 40 minutes. Phase 1 ~10, Phase 2 ~8, Phase 3 ~22.
beats.got: Forty minutes of building a tool. I can see the time, but I cannot see the value yet.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some policy rules can be checked automatically and others need a person. That split is useful to know.

beats.trigger: The customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.
beats.got: I am asked to say what matters in my own company, and that I can do. It is closer to my own material.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: The agent will ask many questions. Someone expects me to sit and answer them.

beats.trigger: hand the rest back: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: When I run out of answers I hand the rest to the agent. Practical, though it sounds like delegating a decision I should own.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/security-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: nothing new. This is IT work. My controller or IT would do the install.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The new check adds to the existing controls and does not replace them. Good, that is the correct answer.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The audit will not give me a pass. It will give me a list and a decision.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: It finds things I missed and marks others as unknown rather than guessing. An honest 'I can't tell' beats a false green.

beats.trigger: Now work the risks. List them, have the agent explain each, what it means in this system, why the rank landed where it did
beats.got: I get a ranked risk list and can question each item. That is close to how I review anything.

beats.trigger: The risk did not go away. That is expected. A mitigation reduces, it does not eliminate.
beats.got: I pick one risk, the agent mitigates it, and the leftover risk is written down. That is something I can show the board.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can actually answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: When I am stuck, I take legal or IT a narrow question plus the evidence. That cuts their time and mine.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent. You must do the work.
beats.got: One mitigation is a demo. A production agent needs all of it done. There is no estimate of how much work that is.

beats.trigger: The unease that remains is what the loop is supposed to produce, not what it failed to remove.
beats.got: The unease is meant to stay. I would rather have a number than a mood.

beats.trigger: "that residual is too vague, name the file or behaviour."
beats.got: I can push back when a recorded residual is vague, and the agent writes rules into its instructions for next time.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable method you can hand to a colleague. It is not a deployed service and owns nothing.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: I have homework: one sentence per case on what check was missing. Short and clear.

beats.trigger: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: The Deloitte Australia report is a real case of an AI-assisted output going wrong in a way that costs money, and it is exactly the kind of case a CFO cares about.

take_homes: Accept the leftover risk on record or close the door. 'Hope it doesn't happen' is not an option.
The cheapest control is not connecting the thing in the first place.
'I can't tell' is a legitimate answer, and when I hit it I take the narrow question and evidence to the owner (legal, IT).

monday.move: Ask IT and legal whether finance data may go into an agent at all. If yes, have my controller try the month-end variance commentary on a read-only copy, with the leftover risk written down.
monday.when: Ask Monday, controller trial within two weeks if IT agrees
monday.stop_condition: IT or legal says no, or the run shows a leak or an invented figure
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data.

misconception.why: I still think of AI as a licence you buy. Hearing that safety comes from reviews, scoping and written decisions that people sign made me see that the organisation has to build the capability. Nobody gave me a cost, so I am not fully moved.

one_line: Honest about residual risk and the best line was 'don't open the door', but no money figures anywhere and the 'uncomfortable feeling' talk is not for me.
